newsitem.title: TURKEY: WGC sees Indian 1996 gold demand rising to 500 T. [corrected 13:17 gmt]
newsitem.headline: WGC sees Indian 1996 gold demand rising to 500 T. [corrected 13:17 gmt]

text.p: Indian gold demand is estimated to rise to about 500 tonnes with the imminent festival season from 477 tonnes (corrects from "447 tonnes") last year and compared to 253 tonnes in the first half of this year, World Gold Council (WGC) said on Wednesday.
"With the festival season ahead of us, (the demand) might well reach 500 tonnes for the full year," said Rolf Schneebeli, WGC's regional chief executive for Middle East and India.
He told the two-day International Gold Markets conference in Istanbul that 228 tonnes of gold was imported by non-resident Indians in 1995, mainly from Dubai, to meet the demand.
India, the largest consumer of the precious metal in the world, is estimated to hold between 8,000 tonnes to 12,000 tonnes of gold in private and public holdings, he said.
Market sources said the demand would pick up over the coming weeks ahead of the Hindu festival of Diwali that starts in November.
Schneebeli said an accelerated rupee depreciation had last year boosted gold bullion purchases in India, where gold is traditionally considered as more of a status symbol than a saving instrument.
"The rupee came under pressure after a long period of relative stability and the gold price in rupees started soaring after September 1995," he said.

"When the international price had its uptick early this year, the Indian demand immediately fell short of expectations after the prices normalised again and is now substantially higher on a year to date basis compared to last year," he said.
He said with good monsoons so far this year farmers expected another good harvest which in turn should boost rural demand for jewellery for the remaining part of the year.

However, he said, the financial sector was getting more advanced and banks are obtaining wider acceptance which might be negative for gold in the longer term as gold savings might be substituted with stocks and time deposits.
He reiterated recent estimates in the market that Indian gold demand could shoot up to 1,000 tonnes a year with an expected 13 million weddings in early years in the new millenium.

He said the Indian government should further liberalise the gold industry to reduce the price premium between local and international prices which fell to 20 percent from 60 to 80 percent after the government allowed imports in 1992.
